conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling during these first weeks and months of motherhood.  

Everything we discuss stays between us unless you tell me otherwise, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you. We’ll go through ten gentle questions about the past seven days; each one usually takes only a moment to answer.  

Whenever you’re ready, we can begin.  

To start: overall, in the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Honestly, most of the time it feels like I have to force it. I’ll smile if someone makes a joke or if my partner tries to cheer me up, but the laughter doesn’t come easily. I used to laugh a lot—now it feels like I’m too tired or just not in the mood.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really. I can manage a chuckle here or there, but it’s definitely harder than it used to be—most things just don’t feel that funny right now.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still get little sparks of excitement—like when my mom says she’s coming over to help, or when I think about taking the baby for a walk if the weather’s nice—but it’s not the same steady “can’t-wait” feeling I used to have. A lot of the time I catch myself thinking, “That’ll be nice… if I have the energy.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that. If the baby’s fussy and I can’t settle him right away, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—maybe I’m not holding him the “right” way or I missed some cue. A couple nights ago he wouldn’t latch, and I lay there crying, telling myself I must be a terrible mom. Rationally I know that’s probably not true, but the thought still pops up.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes, yeah. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly feel this wave of worry—like, what if he stops breathing when I put him down, or what if there’s something wrong the doctor missed? Nothing triggered it, really. It’s not every minute, but it happens a few times a day and my heart races until I check on him again.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week I’ve had that sudden rush—heart pounding, can’t catch my breath—like I’m about to get bad news, but nothing’s actually happening. Once I was just folding laundry while the baby napped and it hit me out of nowhere. It passes after a minute or two, but it’s unsettling.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most days it feels like I’m barely treading water. Between feedings, diapers, trying to sleep myself, and still having chores pile up, I keep thinking, “How does anyone do this?” I’m managing, but it’s that constant sense that one more tiny thing could tip me over the edge.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

It’s not every night, but several nights this week I’ve lain there with my mind racing—mostly worrying about the baby—and I can’t drift off even when he’s asleep. I’m exhausted, yet I’ll stare at the ceiling or keep checking the monitor, and before I know it an hour’s gone by.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do get waves of sadness—like yesterday, when my partner asked how my day was, I just started tearing up and couldn’t explain why. It’s not constant, but it hits me a few times a day, and then it lifts for a while before creeping back.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not a lot—maybe twice this week. Both times it came on suddenly, like when I couldn’t get the baby to settle and felt totally useless. The tears lasted a few minutes and then stopped, but it wasn’t an everyday thing.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I’ve felt overwhelmed and tired, but I haven’t had any thoughts about hurting myself.

You've shared that the past week has felt heavy-laughter comes rarely, excitement is muted, and waves of sadness or worry catch you several times a day. <quote>Most things just don't feel that funny right now</quote>, and even simple tasks feel as though you're <quote>barely treading water</quote>. At the same time, you remain committed to your baby and have not had thoughts of self-harm.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 18, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>The patient reports a clear reduction in ability to laugh and find things funny, aligning with "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports only occasional, muted anticipation that is "not the same" as before, matching "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intense self-blame for normal infant behavior, indicating this occurs "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports spontaneous, recurrent episodes of anxiety several times daily without clear trigger, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, unexplained panic episodes several times this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent daily struggles and feeling on the verge of being overwhelmed, matching 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple nights of racing thoughts and prolonged difficulty falling asleep, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple daily waves of sadness that come and go, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 18 exceeds the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. Key items: Q3 self-blame scored 3, Q8 sadness scored 2, Q1&2 anhedonia scored 2 each, Q4-7&10 anxiety/overwhelm/insomnia all scored 2, giving an 18-point sum. These align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: ≥5 symptoms present (depressed mood, diminished interest, guilt, anxiety, sleep disturbance) causing clinically significant distress. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>OB/GYN</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for full evaluation
2. Begin evidence-based treatment discussion (CBT, IPT, or medication) tailored to breastfeeding preferences
3. Involve supportive partner/family to share night duties and allow 3-4 hour sleep blocks
4. Practice 5-minute paced breathing when panic sensations arise; schedule daily 10-minute outdoor walk
5. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to track treatment response and adjust plan
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 18: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh-based questionnaire, self-report, 0–3 Likert not applied; descriptive answers reviewed.

Symptoms endorsed (frequency & intensity meet screening threshold):  
- Depressed mood: recurrent “waves” of sadness, tearfulness 2×/week, anhedonia (reduced laughter, blunted anticipatory pleasure)  
- Sleep disturbance: initial insomnia related to racing worries, even when infant asleep  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame: interprets infant fussiness as maternal failure; “terrible mom” cognitions  
- Anxiety: multiple daily un-cued worries (infant safety); 2–3 panic-like surges (heart racing, breathlessness) while at rest  
- Feeling overwhelmed: “treading water,” perceives minimal reserve to cope with routine demands  

Negative screening items:  
- No self-harm ideation; no suicidal thoughts reported  

Risk profile:  
Moderate–high for postpartum depression and co-occurring anxiety; no acute safety concerns at present.

Plan:  
Continue monitoring; consider standardized EPDS scoring; referral to OB/GYN or perinatal mental health for evaluation and possible evidence-based intervention (CBT, IPT, or medication consult).
